Male Wistar-rats were exposed to 7.35 mg/cu m zinc-chromate (15930946) dust in an inhalation chamber for 6 hours per day between 8:30 AM and 2:30 PM, or from 11:00 PM to 5:00 AM for four consecutive days. Levels of chromium were analyzed in blood samples drawn immediately before and after exposure and during the following 37 days, and in urine and feces collected from individual rats during and for 24 to 48 hours following exposure. Whole blood chromium levels increased rapidly with exposure time, and fell sharply immediately after cessation of exposure, followed by a more gradual decline. Blood chromium concentrations increased gradually with repeated exposures and appeared to approach a plateau after 4 days of exposure. Blood chromium levels dropped by less than 50 percent during the first 3 days following cessation of exposure; 20 percent of the initial concentration remained after 18 days, and 9 percent remained after 37 days. Urinary excretion of chromium increased rapidly following initiation of exposure and dropped quickly following cessation of exposure, but remained elevated above pre-exposure levels after 3 days. Fecal chromium content increased rapidly after initiation of exposure but fell to near pre-exposure levels within 48 hours after cessation of exposure. There were no significant differences found in blood, urinary or fecal chromium levels between the animals exposed during the day and those exposed at night. The authors conclude that chromium is absorbed quickly during inhalation of soluble chromates and its major route of excretion is in the urine. The persistence of chromium in the blood suggests that chromium exists in the hexavalent state in the blood and is bound to erythrocytes.

StringWithMarkup.String: Zinc can enter the body through the lungs, skin, and gastrointestinal tract. Intestinal absorption of zinc is controlled by zinc carrier protein CRIP. Zinc also binds to metallothioneins, which help prevent absorption of excess zinc. Zinc is widely distributed and found in all tissues and tissues fluids, concentrating in the liver, gastrointestinal tract, kidney, skin, lung, brain, heart, and pancreas. In the bloodstream zinc is found bound to carbonic anhydrase in erythrocytes, as well as bound to albumin, _2-macroglobulin, and amino acids in the the plasma. Albumin and amino acid bound zinc can diffuse across tissue membranes. Zinc is excreted in the urine and faeces. Chromium is absorbed from oral, inhalation, or dermal exposure and distributes to nearly all tissues, with the highest concentrations found in kidney and liver. Bone is also a major storage site and may contribute to long-term retention. Hexavalent chromium's similarity to sulfate and chromate allow it to be transported into cells via sulfate transport mechanisms. Inside the cell, hexavalent chromium is reduced first to pentavalent chromium, then to trivalent chromium by many substances including ascorbate, glutathione, and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. Chromium is almost entirely excreted with the urine. (A12, L16, L49)

Section.Description: The threshold limit value (TLV) of a chemical is an airborne concentration at which a worker can be exposed day after day for a working lifetime without adverse effect. [2] Threshold limit value - short-term exposure limit (TLV-STEL): a 15-minute TWA exposure that should not be exceeded at any time during a workday, even if the 8-hour TWA is within the TLV-TWA. [3] Threshold limit value - ceiling limit (TLV-C): absolute exposure limit that should not be exceeded at any time. TLVs are developed by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienist.  While TLVs are widely accepted occupational exposure limits, they are not standards enforced by the U.S. Government.

StringWithMarkup.String: Anaemia results from the excessive absorption of zinc suppressing copper and iron absorption, most likely through competitive binding of intestinal mucosal cells. Unbalanced levels of copper and zinc binding to Cu,Zn-superoxide dismutase has been linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Stomach acid dissolves metallic zinc to give corrosive zinc chloride, which can cause damage to the stomach lining. Metal fume fever is thought to be an immune response to inhaled zinc. Hexavalent chromium's carcinogenic effects are caused by its metabolites, pentavalent and trivalent chromium. The DNA damage may be caused by hydroxyl radicals produced during reoxidation of pentavalent chromium by hydrogen peroxide molecules present in the cell. Trivalent chromium may also form complexes with peptides, proteins, and DNA, resulting in DNA-protein crosslinks, DNA strand breaks, DNA-DNA interstrand crosslinks, chromium-DNA adducts, chromosomal aberrations and alterations in cellular signaling pathways. It has been shown to induce carcinogenesis by overstimulating cellular regulatory pathways and increasing peroxide levels by activating certain mitogen-activated protein kinases.
